summary: Defines a new TLV that lets IS-IS routers flood their name to system ID mapping across the network, so people see names instead of numbers. This is an informational memo, and it was replaced by RFC 5301.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2763 defines an optional IS-IS field that lets a router advertise a symbolic name along with link-state information. A receiving router may store that name with the system ID, and RFC 5301 later replaced this specification.

questions: how do is-is routers advertise names

subtitle: A way for IS-IS routers to advertise symbolic names with their link-state information

tldr.problem: IS-IS system identifiers are less clear to read than symbolic names, and static name tables must be maintained on every router.
tldr.mechanism: An optional Dynamic Hostname TLV carries a symbolic name in an IS-IS link-state PDU, so other routers can learn the name-to-system-ID mapping.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2763 was later replaced by RFC 5301.

sections.title: Making Router Identifiers Easier to Read
sections.content:
IS-IS uses a system ID to represent a node. Operators may need to inspect adjacencies, routing-table entries and the link-state database, where hexadecimal IDs are less clear than symbolic names.

Static name-to-system-ID mappings require every router to maintain entries for all routers. Changing or adding a router can require configuration changes across the network; the RFC also discusses DNS as an alternative with its own drawbacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use system IDs, but names can be easier for people to recognize in diagnostic information. Static lookup tables must be updated on every router when names or IDs change.

sections.title: The Dynamic Hostname TLV
sections.content:
The RFC defines the Dynamic Hostname Type-Length-Value (TLV) as type 137. Its value is a string from 1 to 255 bytes that names the router originating the link-state PDU (LSP). The RFC recommends using the router's fully qualified domain name or part of it, but permits another string chosen by operators.

The system ID can be derived from the LSP identifier. The TLV may appear in any fragment of a non-pseudo node LSP, and its value is not null-terminated. In a pseudo-node LSP, the name must not be interpreted as the router's DNS hostname.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can include a short name in its link-state message. Other routers can use that name with the system ID taken from the message identifier.

sections.title: Optional Use and Security
sections.content:
The TLV is optional on both sides. A router may include it when it originates an LSP, and a receiving router may ignore it or install the name and system ID in its local mapping table. A router may also include it in a pseudo-node LSP to associate a symbolic name with a local LAN.

The RFC says it raises no new security issues for IS-IS and encourages use of IS-IS authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can choose whether to send or use the name information. The RFC encourages IS-IS authentication and says the proposal raises no new security issues.
